          "chunk_id": "CHUNK_Concentration of Rare Earth Elements During High Temperature Pyrolysis of Waste Printed Circuit Boards_2.2. High temperature pyrolysis_00e5977c",
          "text": "## 2.2. High temperature pyrolysis\nThe heat treatment of waste PCBs was carried out in two different types of furnaces: (a) a horizontal resistance furnace, (b) a thermal plasma furnace. The plasma furnace generates a high level of turbulence in the heating zone, whereas only turbulence in the horizontal furnace was caused by the continuous flow of inert gas (1 L/min). Heat treatment temperatures were chosen to be approximately850 ^∘C as the generation of harmful dioxins/furans generated from waste PCBs becomes negligibly small at temperatures above 700 \u0001C (Saini et al., 2017). Higher temperatures (above the melting point of copper: 1085 \u0001C) were not considered necessary based on our previous experience on the recovery of copper from waste PCBs, as these led to enhanced mixing and the formation of mixed alloys (Cayumil et al., 2014). Operational details of the two furnaces are provided next.\nA schematic representation of the horizontal resistance furnace is given in Fig. 2a. Basic characteristics of this furnace were as follows: furnace length: 1200 mm; heating zone: 630 mm long, 54 mm diameter, 3 mm wall thickness; heating rate: up to 40 \u0001C/min, sample weight: up to 0.02 kg; Gas flow: Ar gas at 1 L/min. Waste PCB pieces were placed on the sample holder and the furnace was heated to 850 \u0001C, held at that temperature for 15 min (up to 60 min in some cases), and then furnace cooled. Pyrolysis residues were collected for further characterization.\nA schematic representation of the thermal plasma furnace shown in Fig. 2b. This pot type 35 kW DC extended transfer arc plasma reactor uses zircon coated graphite crucible as the furnace hearth. DC transferred arc plasma was used to create high energy density/temperatures between the two graphite electrodes arranged in a vertical configuration (Gomez et al., 2009). Size reduced PCBs were placed in the graphite crucible of the plasma reactor. The plasma furnace was operated using 100 A current and a DC voltage of 50 V. Argon gas was passed continuously through the furnace at a flow rate of 1 L/min with typical heating rates 750 \u0001C/min. The reactor was closed at the top with a graphite lid and was thermally insulated. The assembly of the graphite crucible and the bottom electrode together (the ‘anode’), was kept stationary during the furnace operation. The formation and the stabilization of the extended arc plasma were carried out by the movement of the top electrode (the ‘cathode’) using a rack and pinion mechanism. An arc was created by the electrical breakdown of gases; extreme heat generated stripped electrons from gas molecules resulting in an ionized gas or plasma. A water cooling system at the end of two electrodes was used to prevent excessive heating.\nWaste PCBs were heat treated at 850 ^∘C for 15 min, and the pyrolysis residues were collected after the furnace had cooled down. While the gas flow rates were maintained at 1L/min for both furnaces, the heating rates were significantly different due to differences in furnace operations.",

          "chunk_id": "CHUNK_Concentration of Rare Earth Elements During High Temperature Pyrolysis of Waste Printed Circuit Boards_5. Concluding remarks_1adc5324",
          "text": "## 5. Concluding remarks\nIn-depth investigations were carried out on the recovery of wide range of REEs from waste PCBs using resistance as well as thermal plasma furnaces. Key findings of this investigation are summarized below:\n1. Waste PCBs were found to be a valuable resource of REEs. Light REEs recovered included La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce, heavy REEs Dy and Y. Three of the REEs recovered, i.e., Nd, Dy and Y were from among the list of most critical material resources.\n2. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the slag rich carbonaceous fraction with negligible levels detected in the copper rich as well as in the tin/lead rich metallic fractions. This result was observed for all PCBs under investigation and for both types of furnaces.\n3. A wide variation was observed in the concentrations of REEs recovered from PCBs under investigation. There were no specific correlations between the level of REEs recovered and the type of PCB. The REE recovery was generally poor from RAM boards as compared to the corresponding recoveries mobiles, mother boards and power supply boards.\n4. Turbulence was found to play an important role in enhancing the yield from waste PCBs. Much higher levels of REEs were recovered after pyrolysis in the thermal plasma furnace, with inherently high turbulence levels within the furnace. The recoveries were much smaller after pyrolysis in the resistance furnace with little local turbulence. By using plasma furnace, REE recovery yields showed increases ranging from 118% to 2500% for various elements.\n5. With the recoveries of a wide variety of REEs from waste PCBs, this study has shown that pyrolysis residues (slag rich carbonaceous phase) from waste PCBs have the potential to become a valuable urban mining resource for REEs, especially for those economies with little or no REE resources of their own.\n6. By recovering REEs in addition to precious and other metals from waste PCBs, this novel study has helped enhance the economic viability and profitability of recycling electronic waste. These findings are expected to play an important role in making recycling a key player in the management of burgeoning volumes of electronic waste, and towards sustainable developments in the field.",

Key findings of this investigation are summarized below:\n1. Waste PCBs were found to be a valuable resource of REEs. Light REEs recovered included La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce, heavy REEs Dy and Y. Three of the REEs recovered, i.e., Nd, Dy and Y were from among the list of most critical material resources.\n2. The REE recovery was generally poor from RAM boards as compared to the corresponding recoveries mobiles, mother boards and power supply boards.\n4.
